evidence: `applying` is a store field this PR introduced; the selectSession reset enumerates the other four new fields (analyzerMetadata/Results/Running/pipeline) and omits it, so an apply that threw or was abandoned leaves the next session's Apply and Save buttons disabled. The cited law is about two divergable representations of one concept; a reset that forgets one flag is incompleteness, not a second clock.
guidance_note: When adding a transient flag to a store, add it to every reset function in the same edit - enumerate the resets from the state shape, do not append to whichever one is on screen.

evidence: The pre-fix body cleared `applying` at each of several exits with no catch around the `window.electronAPI.invoke` await, so a rejected invoke leaks the flag; and the post-await block re-read `get().selectedSession`/`selectedProvider` rather than the values the apply was issued against, so a mid-flight session switch reloaded the new session's state from the old apply's result.
guidance_note: Write the exit-path cleanup and the stale-target guard at the same moment you write an await inside a store action; both are properties of the await, not follow-up work.

evidence: The block comment claimed 'Slice 1 has no force flag - when pipeline output fails structural validation, the apply is refused' while the signature immediately below it read `applyPipeline(pipeline: Pipeline, force = false)` and force was wired to two dialogs' Force-save buttons.
guidance_note: When you add a parameter, re-read and update the block comment above the function in the same edit - the comment is part of the signature's surface.

evidence: `STEP_KIND_LABEL: Record<string, ...>` over a closed `StepKind` union accepts any key and requires none, so adding a third StepKind would compile with no UI label; the fix's `Record<StepKind, ...>` makes the omission a compile error, which is precisely what the cited law asks the type to carry.
guidance_note: Type every per-variant lookup table as Record<TheUnion, T> at the moment the table is written, so the union's growth is checked rather than reviewed.

evidence: `pipelineEffectsForIndex(steps, index)` was called from every rendered MessageRow and linearly scanned each step's targets, so cost was O(messages x steps x targets) on every render of a session that can hold thousands of messages. The replacement (a memoized index->kinds Map) is right, but it silently changed per-step semantics and produced F25.
guidance_note: Derive per-row lookups once at the parent with useMemo whenever the row count scales with session size, instead of giving each row a scan.

evidence: The op re-serialized every targeted line with JSON.stringify even when `filter(b => b.type !== 'thinking')` removed nothing, so key order and whitespace of untouched messages could change and inflate the recorded version diff. Preserving the raw bytes keeps the source line as the one authoritative representation, so the citation fits.
guidance_note: A transformer that can be a no-op must return the input bytes unchanged rather than a re-serialization of them; compare before/after and short-circuit at the point you write the transform.

evidence: Same defect as F1 at the clearSession reset, which likewise lists the new analyzer fields and omits `applying`; raised in the same round as F1, so it cost no extra round, but the reviewer had to name both sites because the first edit only covered one.
guidance_note: Treat 'reset the editor state' as one list with several call sites: change the list, then apply it to every site, rather than editing the site the finding names.

evidence: The race was real: the pre-fix body captured `filePath` once but later called `ensureBaselineForActive()` and `activeProviderId()`, which re-read module globals after the readFile/writeFile awaits. The agent snapshotted adapter/path/provider at function entry instead of making the IPC session-addressed as asked; since ipcMain dispatches handlers in arrival order and the snapshot is synchronous at entry, an apply issued before a switch still binds to the right file, so the narrower fix is sufficient. The finding is on original-PR logic - a1fe4fd only rewrote the docstring above it for F3 - so the post-review-commit flag is proximity, not causation.
guidance_note: When you snapshot ambient state at a function's entry, grep the whole body for the other ambient accessors and snapshot all of them at once; capturing the first one you notice is what left this race.

evidence: The inner block asserted 'force only bypasses structural validation, never live-tail' while `liveTailGate(filePath, force)` early-returns unblocked when force is true - and the docstring twelve lines above, rewritten by the F3 fix one round earlier, now said the opposite. F3's fix corrected one stale force-semantics comment in this function and left its twin.
guidance_note: When correcting a stale comment, grep the enclosing function for every other comment making a claim about the same parameter before you push.

evidence: The reviewer's mechanism cannot occur: `const running = new Set(get().analyzerRunning); running.add(id); set({analyzerRunning: running})` has no await between the read and the write, and Zustand's set is synchronous, so concurrent runAnalyzer calls cannot interleave and drop ids. The agent applied the functional form anyway and said so - the right split answer for a costless robustness change on a false premise. Verified the code is byte-identical at a0b6591, so the post-review-commit flag is the surrounding file being edited, not this logic.
guidance_note: State the interleaving point (which await lets another continuation run) before accepting a race finding, so a costless style change is not recorded as a bug fix.

evidence: Same analysis as F10: `const after = get(); ... set({analyzerResults: {...after.analyzerResults, [id]: result}})` runs with no await between the read and the set, so no lost update is possible; the reply carries F10's 'safe today, functional form is future-proof' justification by reference. runAnalyzer is unchanged from a0b6591, so the flag is proximity.

Real bug: handleSave called `addStep(...)` into the stored pipeline before applying, and a blocked apply returns with `markedForRemoval` still populated, so the user's retry appended a second identical remove-messages step. The agent took the reviewer's own third option (build a one-off pipeline, never mutate stored state) and added a double-click regression test. The shim is original-PR code, so the post-review-commit flag is proximity.
guidance_note: Build a mutation's payload as a local value at call time; never stage it into shared store state that survives a failed attempt.

evidence: Verified regression: both ops resolve targets through `buildSourceIndexToUuid`, which parses Claude JSONL and keys on `uuid`, so a Gemini session's 'Remove N & Save' would have written back unchanged content and still recorded a version. The routing of all providers through applyPipeline is original-PR design, not a product of F12's fix. The cited law is misapplied: the fix is `if (selectedProvider !== 'claude') { save(); return; }` - variability in whether operations run, which is exactly what the law forbids; the lawful shape is a provider-keyed mutation table, and this untyped fork went on to generate F14, F17, F18 and F29.
guidance_note: Before routing an existing path through a new mechanism, list every input class the old path served and check the new mechanism covers each; where it does not, express the split as a provider-keyed table rather than an if.

evidence: The premise held: main-side applyPipeline ran Claude-only ops against whatever session was active and would write and version a file for any provider. The agent declined the main-side gate, arguing 'the IPC contract is consistent with the renderer's dispatch' - i.e. leaving a main-process invariant enforced only by the renderer. Seven rounds later F29 raised the identical point and the agent then added exactly this guard, so the decline bought nothing and cost a round.
guidance_note: When a caller-side fix is offered in place of a check at the boundary that owns the invariant, add the check at the boundary; a renderer is not a trusted enforcer for main.

evidence: runAllAnalyzers awaited `session:list-analyzers` then unconditionally wrote analyzerMetadata/Results/Running, so a provider switch during that await committed the wrong provider's analyzer catalog. The F2 fix one round earlier had applied precisely this stale-session guard to applyPipeline in the same file and left runAllAnalyzers as the only remaining unguarded async action (verified unchanged at a0b6591).
guidance_note: When you add a stale-target guard to one async action in a store, sweep every other action in that file that awaits and guard them in the same commit.

evidence: The remove-step button renders only the glyph 'x' with a `title` attribute; title is not a reliable accessible name across screen readers, and the sibling chevron in the same file already carried an aria-label, so the file was internally inconsistent.
guidance_note: Give an icon-only control its aria-label in the same line you write the icon, matching the pattern already used elsewhere in the file.

evidence: The F13 fix reintroduced the legacy `save()` path for non-Claude providers but left the Save button's disabled state and label reading only `applying`, which that path never sets - so a Gemini save showed an enabled 'Remove N & Save' button throughout the write. The fix (`applying || saving`) is a union of values with no branch, so the law citation fits here.
guidance_note: When you restore a second execution path, re-wire every UI signal that path owns - in-flight, error, result - in the same edit that restores it.

evidence: The dialog wiring in this hunk was written by the F13 fix: it changed onForceSave to `handleSave(true)`, which can route to the legacy `save()`, while leaving `saving={applying}`, so both dialogs' Force-save buttons stayed enabled during a non-Claude forced write. Same missed sweep as F17, in the same round.
guidance_note: Grep for every consumer of a flag before you replace it with another; the F13 edit swapped the mutation path and left three readers of the old flag behind.

evidence: Real: the store's applyPipeline rethrows invoke failures after clearing `applying`, and `onClick={handleApply}` hands React a promise it never observes, so an IPC failure surfaces as an unhandled rejection. handleApply is original-PR code, so the post-review-commit flag is proximity. The accepted fix logs and swallows, which removes the warning but leaves an IPC failure invisible to the user - a weaker outcome than surfacing it.
guidance_note: Decide the failure path when you write an async click handler: void-wrap the call and choose surface-or-swallow in the same edit, rather than leaving the promise floating.

evidence: Confirmed against source-index.ts at a0b6591: `targetUuidsForStep(source, targets)` called `buildSourceIndexToUuid(source)` internally, so every op re-split and re-JSON.parsed the entire session file - O(steps x lines) parses for a file that can be tens of megabytes. Hoisting the map into runPipeline and passing it to ops is the correct shape.
guidance_note: Resolve a shared index once at the loop head and pass it into the callees, rather than giving each callee raw content and letting it rebuild the index.

evidence: handleSave awaited `save()`/`applyPipeline()` with no catch behind the `() => void handleSave()` onClick that an earlier fix had added - the identical shape the F19 fix had just corrected in PipelinePanel.handleApply one round earlier. The agent's own reply concedes it: 'Same shape as PipelinePanel's handleApply from the previous round.'
guidance_note: When a fix is a pattern rather than a point change, apply it to every handler of that shape in the diff in the same commit, not only the one the reviewer named.

evidence: Verified both halves: `ClaudeLine.uuid` is `uuid?: string` and buildSourceIndexToUuid maps only uuid-bearing visible lines, while the legacy adapter's visibleLines() pairs every visible line with its physical index - so the mechanism the reviewer describes is real. But scanning six real Claude Code session files on this machine (~7,000 visible messages) found zero visible messages without a uuid, so the 'functional regression' does not fire on real input, and the uuid anchoring is what makes step order irrelevant, so the pushback on a positional fallback is right. The residual miss is that the no-op stays invisible to the user (console.warn in main, not surfaced). buildSourceIndexToUuid is byte-identical to a0b6591 - only targetUuidsForStep's signature changed in 8472eb4 - so the flag is the file being touched, not fix-caused logic.
guidance_note: When a resolver silently drops inputs it cannot map, decide at write time whether the drop is surfaced or swallowed and encode that in the return type, rather than leaving a silent no-op for a reviewer to find.

evidence: The pre-population is genuinely redundant - each runAnalyzer adds its own id synchronously on entry - but the cost is one extra set() per catalog load, not the rerender storm the finding implies; removing it is harmless. The pre-population is original-PR code (verified at a0b6591), unchanged by the round-1 and round-2 edits to the same function, so the flag is proximity.

The comment written by the F2 fix reads 'try/finally pattern: applying is the gate ... clearing it on every exit path' while the code it annotates is a try/catch that clears and rethrows, with the clear duplicated across five exits - the comment described the design the fix aspired to, not the one it shipped. The agent then implemented the actual try/finally.
guidance_note: Write the comment against the code you actually produced: if the comment names a pattern, implement that pattern in the same edit or name the one you used.

evidence: A behavioral regression introduced by the F5 perf fix: the replaced `pipelineEffectsForIndex` tested `step.targets.includes(index)` and therefore contributed one kind per step regardless of duplicates, while `buildPipelineEffectMap` iterates `for (const idx of step.targets)` and pushes once per occurrence - so a duplicated target now renders duplicate badges and inflates totalTargets. The pre-fix code had this right.
guidance_note: When replacing a membership test with an iteration over the same collection, preserve the set semantics the test implied - iterate over new Set(targets), not the raw array.

evidence: formatPipelineLabel counted `s.targets.length` while the ops act on a deduped uuid Set, so a duplicated target inflated the version label recorded on disk relative to what actually changed. The previous round's F25 fix deduped the UI's effect map and totalTargets and left this third consumer of the same field counting raw length.
guidance_note: When you rule out duplicates at one consumer of a field, fix every consumer that counts or displays that field in the same commit - grep the field name, do not fix the site the reviewer pointed at.

evidence: The gap is real - `session:run-analyzer` accepted any analyzer id and any path with no provider check while its sibling `session:list-analyzers` is provider-scoped - but the exploit path is narrow because the renderer only ever requests ids that listing returned; this is boundary hygiene rather than a live defect. The handler registration is original-PR code, so the flag is proximity.
guidance_note: Register sibling IPC channels with the same scoping check in one pass; a channel that trusts an argument its neighbour validates is a gap by construction.

evidence: The F27 fix rewrote this handler to validate the analyzer's provider and left the renderer-supplied `filePath` unvalidated, so a stale or wrong path still selected the file the analyzer read - unlike every other editor channel, which takes the active path from main. Same 'is this request scoped to the active session' question, one dimension checked and one not, in the handler the fix had just touched.
guidance_note: When you add a scoping check to a handler, check every argument that names a target - provider and path - not the single dimension the reviewer mentioned.

evidence: Identical to F14 seven rounds earlier, where the agent declined the main-side gate on the grounds that the renderer never routes non-Claude sessions to this channel; here he implemented it. The F27 fix the round before had also added exactly this guard to the sibling channel registered three lines above and did not extend it to apply-pipeline. Note the agent's justification, 'defense-in-depth with the renderer-side handleSave dispatch', is the two-checkpoints shape [LAW:single-enforcer] refuses - the correct reading is that the IPC boundary is the single enforcer and the renderer dispatch is the duplicate.
guidance_note: Put the invariant check at the boundary that owns it the first time it is raised; a check the renderer performs and main does not is not enforced, and calling the boundary check 'defense in depth' inverts the single-enforcer question of where the rule lives.

evidence: The stale-session guard added by the F2 fix skipped the post-apply state writes but still returned the real SessionSaveResult, and SessionEditor feeds that into setSaveResult - so after a session switch the user could be shown the old session's validation or live-tail dialog and force-save it against the new one. The guard's own comment said 'Drop the result' while the code returned it.
guidance_note: A stale-request guard must neutralize the return value as well as skip the local writes - the caller acts on what you hand back, not on your reason for handing it back.

evidence: The template read `${n} message${n === 1 ? '' : 's'} have thinking blocks`, so the singular case rendered '1 message have ...'; the same file already used a has/have ternary elsewhere. Original-PR text, so the flag is proximity.
guidance_note: Pluralize the verb inside the same conditional expression that pluralizes the noun, rather than pluralizing the noun alone.

narrative: Twelve review rounds for a 2241-line feature PR, and the agent accepted 26 of 31 findings outright - the reviewer was right about most things, and the agent's fixes were mostly sound. What made this expensive is that eleven findings existed because an earlier fix was applied to exactly the site the reviewer named and nowhere else: the stale-guard sweep missed runAllAnalyzers (F15), the void-wrap-plus-catch sweep missed handleSave (F21), the duplicate-target dedupe missed the version label (F26), the IPC provider guard missed the sibling channel (F29), and the F5 perf rewrite silently regressed the duplicate handling its predecessor got right (F25). Rounds 6, 7 and 9 contained nothing but fix-caused findings and would not have happened at all. Two decisions cost the most: the provider fork in F13, an if-branch blessed with [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] while being exactly what that law forbids, which then generated F14, F17, F18 and F29; and the F14 decline of a main-process boundary check on the grounds that the renderer already routes correctly, which the agent reversed seven rounds later.
guidance_observations: Every fix was scoped to the line the reviewer cited; nothing in the agent's process asks 'where else does this shape appear in my own diff', and that single missing step accounts for the majority of this PR's rounds.

The agent cited a law in eight replies and three of the citations were decorative or inverted - [LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] to justify an if-branch on provider, [LAW:one-source-of-truth] for a forgotten reset field - which means a law token in a reply is not evidence the law was consulted before the code was written.

Twice the agent argued a boundary check was unnecessary because a caller already behaves correctly (F14 on apply-pipeline, and the 'IPC contract is consistent with the renderer's dispatch' framing), and both times he later added the check anyway; guidance should make a declined boundary check cost more than an accepted one.

The two findings whose premises were false (F10, F11) were concurrency claims the agent could disprove in one sentence, and he did - while still applying the change; that split answer is the right pattern and cost nothing, but the reply-hint records it as a plain accept.

Three rounds were spent on comments contradicting code the agent had just written (F3, F9, F24), all of them comments the same agent authored in the same PR - the doc-drift is self-inflicted within a single session, not inherited.
